'''Nina Alexandrovna Andreyeva''' ({{langx|ru|Нина Александровна Андреева}}; 12 October 1938 – 24 July 2020) was a [[Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|Soviet Russian]] chemical scientist, teacher, author, and political activist.<ref>{{cite book|title=Encyclopedia of Russian history|year=2004|publisher=Thomson Gale|location=Detroit|isbn=0028659074|pages=v. 1, p. 60|editor=James R. Millar|url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofru0001unse}}</ref> A supporter of classical [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] principles, she wrote an essay entitled ''{{ill|I Cannot Forsake My Principles|ru|Не могу поступаться принципами}}''  that defended many aspects of the traditional Soviet system, and criticized [[General Secretary]] [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] and his closest supporters for not being true [[Communism|communists]]. In the rebuke published in the official party newspaper ''[[Pravda]]'' the essay was called ''The Manifesto of Anti-[[Perestroika]] Forces''.<ref>Quote: "...вопросы подняты серьезные и в таком ключе, который иначе как идейной платформой, манифестом антиперестроечных сил не назовешь. "</ref><ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1988/05/05/world/new-ferment-on-the-pariah-of-perestroika.html "New Ferment On the Pariah Of Perestroika"], ''NY Times''</ref>

== Career in chemistry ==
She was born in [[Leningrad]] (now [[St. Petersburg]]), and was a chemistry lecturer at the [[Leningrad Technological Institute]]. She joined the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]] (CPSU) around 1966.<ref>{{cite news|last=Keller|first=Bill|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/06/26/world/evolution-in-europe-a-neo-stalinist-yearns-for-old-times.html|title=Evolution in Europe; A Neo-Stalinist Yearns for Old Times|work=The New York Times|date=26 June 1990|access-date=5 January 2021|quote=A Communist Party member for 24 of her 51 years, Mrs. Andreyeva says she thinks of quitting the party to help form one with a real Marxist-Leninist backbone.}}</ref>

== ''I Cannot Forsake My Principles'' ==
Andreyeva's essay ''I Cannot Forsake My Principles'' (''{{lang|ru|Не могу поступаться принципами}}''; variously translated in English commentary) was published in the newspaper ''[[Sovetskaya Rossiya]]'' on March 13, 1988, at a time when [[Mikhail Gorbachev|Gorbachev]] and [[Alexander Nikolaevich Yakovlev|Alexander Yakovlev]] were either about to start on overseas visit or already abroad, and was initiated and approved by the secretary of the Communist Party's [[Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union|Central Committee]], [[Yegor Ligachev]].<ref name="Skillen126">{{cite book|last=Skillen|first=Daphne|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qUAlDwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Nina+Andreyeva%22&pg=PA126|title=Freedom of Speech: Politics and Media from Gorbachev to Putin|location=London & New York City|publisher=Routledge|year=2017|pages=126–127|isbn=9781317659891}}</ref> She was contemptuous of [[Perestroika]] and defended the Soviet leader [[Joseph Stalin]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Gutterman|first=Steve|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/week-in-russia-death-andreyeva-anti-perestroika-icon-vagner-riddle-belarus/30759332.html|title=The Week In Russia: The Death Of An Anti-Perestroika Icon And A Wagnerian Riddle In Belarus|work=Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty|date=31 July 2020|access-date=5 January 2021}}</ref> Of the [[Great Purge]]s, "they are being blown out of proportion" she wrote.<ref name="WaPo19890728">{{cite news|last=Remnick|first=David|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1989/07/28/gorbachevs-furious-critic/7d3052c7-b15f-46cd-a2a5-4ba52027fe17/|title=Gorbachev's Furious Critic|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=28 July 1989|access-date=5 January 2021}}</ref>

[[Giulietto Chiesa]], then Moscow correspondent of the Italian Communist newspaper ''[[L'Unità]],'' found Andreyeva's original letter and discovered that it had been rewritten, only 5 pages of her 18-page typescript were published, much of the rest being thought too extreme. In the originally unpublished portions, Andreyeva commented that Stalin's critics wrote "in the language of Goebbels" and referred to "nations of little importance, like the Crimean Tartars and Zionist Jews."<ref name="Skillen126" />

Party officials critical of the reforms welcomed the published essay. Ligachev told the official news agency [[TASS]] to send the Andreyeva letter to local newspapers throughout the Soviet Union to publish it.<ref>Skillen, p. 128</ref> It was much reprinted in the Soviet Union and East Germany, but it received no critical response in the media. The Leningrad party issued a television documentary apparently showing mass support in the city for the Andreyeva letter.<ref>{{cite news|last=Goldman|first=Marshall L.|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-28-me-2752-story.html|title=Wide Bitterness at Gorbachev's Glasnost Shouts Through|work=Los Angeles Times|date=April 28, 1988|access-date=January 5, 2021|quote=But the ''Pravda'' reply indicates how far the Soviet Union has to go before there is real glasnost in the Soviet Union. It took three weeks for the reply to appear.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Keller|first=Bill|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/05/05/world/new-ferment-on-the-pariah-of-perestroika.html|title=New Ferment On the Pariah Of Perestroika|work=The New York Times|date=5 May 1988|access-date=5 January 2021|quote=For three weeks, even the most daring Soviet editors did not publish a response.}}</ref>

Not until after Gorbachev had returned from abroad, and following a two-day meeting of the [[Politburo of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union|politburo]] on March 24–25 to discuss the Andreyeva letter, did a response appear in ''[[Pravda]]'' on 5 April 1988.<ref name="Skillen126" /><ref>{{cite book|last=Taubman|first=William|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iNDADQAAQBAJ&dq=Andreyeva+Ligachev+company&pg=PT290|title=Gorbachev: His Life and Times|location=London|publisher=Simon & Schuster|year=2017|page=290|isbn=9781471128622}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Brown|first=Archie|authorlink=Archie Brown (historian)|title=The Rise and Fall of Communism|year=2009|publisher=Ecco|location=New York City|isbn=978-0-06-113879-9|pages=[https://archive.org/details/risefallofcommun00brow/page/504 504–506]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/risefallofcommun00brow/page/504}}</ref> The ''Pravda'' article described the letter as containing "nostalgia, backward-looking patriotism," the work of "blind, die-hard, undoubting dogmatists."<ref name="WaPo19890728" /> Gorbachev stated that there were mixed reactions to the article within the politburo, with members such as  [[Vitaly Vorotnikov|Vorotnikov]] and Ligachev characterizing the article as an understandable reaction to the negative view of the Soviet past.<ref>Gorbachev, M. S. (1996). Memoirs. New York: Doubleday.</ref> Gorbachev described it as a direct attack "against perestroika."<ref>{{cite book|last=Dobbs|first=Michael|author-link=Michael Dobbs (journalist)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BXoxAAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Nina+Andreyeva%22&pg=PA202|title=Down with Big Brother: The Fall of the Soviet Empire|location=London|publisher=Bloomsbury|year=1997|page=202|isbn=9781408851029}}</ref>

"A year and a half later, [[Yevgeny Dodolev|Evgeny Dodolev]] was able to charm Andreeva—possibly on false pretenses—into sitting for a longform interview for ''[[Vzglyad (Russian TV program)|Vzgliad]]"''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Post-Soviet Public Sphere |url=https://postsoviet90s.com/ |access-date=2026-10-15 |website=Multimedia Sourcebook of the Russian 1990s |language=en}}</ref>

Under the reforms, she told [[David Remnick]] of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' in 1989 that under Stalin "the country built socialism for 30 years" and stated: "Our media are lying about Stalin now. They are blackening our history." On then current conditions, she told him: "The political structure of an anti-socialist movement is taking place in the form of democratic unions and popular fronts."<ref name="WaPo19890728" /> She said of Leningrad television: "they'll show an artist, a painter, who is supposedly a representative of Russian art. But excuse me, he is not a Russian. He is a Jew." She added: "You can say Russian, Ukrainian, why not Jew? Does it diminish the person? Why hide him behind some other nationality. Jew and Zionist mean different things, but all Zionists are Jews." In the ''Sovetskaya Rossiya'' letter, she attacked [[rootless cosmopolitan|"cosmopolitan"]] conspirators.<ref name="WaPo19890728" />

For his book ''[[Lenin's Tomb: The Last Days of the Soviet Empire]]'' (1993), Remnick drew on his contact with Andreyeva.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Remnick |first1=David |title=Lenin's Tomb |date=1993 |publisher=Random House |location=New York City |pages=74–84}}</ref>

==Subsequent career==
By July 1990, she was heading an organization called ''Yedinstvo'' (Unity) which aimed to return the country to the Bolshevik principles of [[Lenin]] and was planning to leave the CPSU.<ref>{{cite news|last=Shanker|first=Tom|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1990-07-08-9002250564-story.html|title=Science Teacher Says Stalin Had It Right All Along|work=Chicago Tribune|date=July 8, 1990|access-date=5 January 2021}}</ref> ''[[The New York Times]]'' described the group in August 1991 as "a haven for many hard-line Communists".<ref>{{cite news|last=Barringer|first=Felicity|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/08/31/world/soviet-turmoil-communist-party-dead-hard-liner-says-just-wait-until-soviet.html|title=Soviet Turmoil; Communist Party Dead? Hard-Liner Says Just Wait Until Soviet Winter|work=The New York Times|date=31 August 1991|access-date=5 January 2021}}</ref>

Andreyeva later played a leadership role in the formation of post-Soviet communist organisations. Founded in November 1991, the [[All-Union Communist Party of Bolsheviks (1991)|All-Union Communist Party of Bolsheviks]] (initially Bolshevik Platform), Andreyeva was the party general secretary and the party wanted a mass campaign to replace [[Boris Yeltsin]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cia.gov/library/readingroom/docs/DOC_0000837998.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160925031904/https://www.cia.gov/library/readingroom/docs/DOC_0000837998.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 25, 2016|title=Russian Political Parties: APrimer|publisher=Central Intelligence Agency|date=1 April 1992|access-date=5 January 2021|page=14}}</ref> It saw itself as the successor to the CPSU. In October 1993, the party was temporarily suspended along with fifteen other organisations after President Yeltsin's repression implemented after a [[1993 Russian constitutional crisis|constitutional crisis]]. In May 1995 she was removed from the post as the head of the [[Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]] [[Central Committee]] of the party for "lack of revolutionary activity."<ref>{{cite book|title=Encyclopedia of Russian history|year=2004|publisher=Thomson Gale|location=Detroit|isbn=0028659074|pages=v. 1, p. 61|editor=James R. Millar|url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofru0001unse}}</ref>

Nina Andreyeva died in [[St. Petersburg]] on 24 July 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://iz.ru/1040101/2020-07-26/umerla-avtor-manifesta-antiperestroechnykh-sil-nina-andreeva|title=Умерла автор "манифеста антиперестроечных сил" Нина Андреева|date=26 July 2020}}</ref>
